card.text: Deal 1 damage to a friendly unit. Deal 4 damage to a random enemy unit.
card.flavorText: When the war reached Soviet cities in 1941, urban combat required new tactics. First developed by the 62nd Army's 13th Guards Rifle Division in Stalingrad, the Soviet shturmovye gruppy (English: assault groups) were elite shock troops assembled to clear and capture fortified buildings and locations through fast close-quarters attacks. These small, flexible units changed street fighting with their specialized three-group structure. The assault group consisted of 6 to 8 men carrying PPSh submachine guns, grenades and sharpened spades. Their standard tactic was to infiltrate as closely as possible, then sprint to the building under covering fire. The assault group would toss grenades into doors and windows, then head inside to finish off the stunned German defenders in hand-to-hand combat.  Right behind them came the reinforcement group with heavy machine guns, mortars, sniper and anti-tank rifles. They transformed captured buildings into strongholds to defend against German counterattacks. Finally, the reserve group provided critical support by laying down covering fire, delivering ammunition and reinforcing failed attacks when needed. The Shturmovye Gruppy encouraged individual initiative and teamwork by pairing soldiers. Unlike traditional mass assaults, these units exploited German weaknesses, especially their fear of night fighting and close combat. These units became very efficient tools for the Red Army in urban warfare, using speed, surprise and overwhelming force to clear buildings room by room. By the time of the Berlin offensive in 1945, Soviet assault groups tactics had been mastered and widespread.
